Non-Hodgkin & Hodgkin Lymphoma

Updated Oct 9, 2026 Revision 1.0 10 learning objectives

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Classify lymphoid neoplasms and name the ones that behave as both leukemia and lymphoma.
  2. LO 2Explain how immunophenotyping and other ancillary tests diagnose lymphoid neoplasms.
  3. LO 3Contrast low-grade (indolent) and high-grade (aggressive) lymphoid neoplasms.
  4. LO 4Define each major B- and T-cell lymphoma by cell of origin, markers, genetics and morphology.
  5. LO 5Describe the presentation, course and complications of each of those lymphomas.
  6. LO 6Outline the classification of Hodgkin lymphoma.
  7. LO 7Describe the Reed-Sternberg cell and its variants, including markers.
  8. LO 8Explain how Hodgkin lymphoma develops and the role of EBV.
  9. LO 9Compare the pathology and clinical features of the five Hodgkin subtypes.
  10. LO 10Distinguish Hodgkin from non-Hodgkin lymphoma by clinical features, grade and stage.

MAPThe lymphoid neoplasm map: sort by speed, then match the marker

LO 1Classifying lymphoid neoplasms

Q1. What is the difference between a leukemia and a lymphoma?

Leukemia

  • Mainly bone marrow + circulating tumor cells
  • Acute = immature precursors; chronic = mature cells

Lymphoma

  • Clonal lymphocytes forming masses in nodes or extranodal sites
  • Marrow involvement = higher stage
  • Both forms of one disease: CLL = SLL (blood vs node); mycosis fungoides → Sézary when cells circulate; ATLL
  • Location, not biology, decides the name
In-house exam

Disorders that are both leukemia and lymphoma: CLL/SLL, mycosis fungoides/Sézary, ATLL (and lymphoblastic ALL/LBL).

Q2. How is the WHO classification organized?
  • B ≫ T: most lymphoid neoplasms are B-cell
  • Each tumor mimics a normal stage of B- or T-cell development
  • Hodgkin = few Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background; NHL = everything else
  • Precursor (lymphoblastic) neoplasms = ALL, covered with the acute leukemias

Normal node

  • Follicles with germinal centers and mantles

Lymphoma vs carcinoma

  • Fish-flesh, soft (lymphoma) vs hard, white (carcinoma)
High yield — risk factors
  • Immunodeficiency: HIV, transplant, Wiskott-Aldrich
  • Autoimmune disease (chronic stimulation): Sjögren, Hashimoto
  • Infection: H. pylori, EBV, HHV-8, HTLV-1, HCV
Memory tool

Lymphoma nodes are soft, rubbery, painless; metastatic carcinoma is hard and fixed; infection is tender and localized.

LO 2Immunophenotyping and ancillary tests

Q1. How is a lymphoid neoplasm diagnosed?
  1. Biopsy: node, marrow or tissue (B and T cells look alike, so morphology alone isn't enough)
  2. Immunophenotype: flow cytometry or IHC for CD markers
  3. Clonality: one light chain only (κ or λ), or clonal Ig/TCR gene rearrangement
  4. Cytogenetics / molecular: FISH or PCR for translocations
High yield — monoclonality

All κ (or all λ) = monoclonal → neoplasm. Mixed κ + λ = polyclonal → reactive.

Q2. Which markers matter?
NeoplasmMarkers
All B cellsCD19, CD20 (pan-B); CD10 = germinal center
CLL/SLLCD19, CD20, CD23, CD5
Mantle cellCD5, CD19, CD20, cyclin D1; CD23−

Step 1

CD5+ B cell? Only two: CLL (CD23+) and mantle cell (CD23−, cyclin D1+). CD10+ B cell: follicular, Burkitt (± DLBCL).

Q3. Which translocations should I know?

Most non-random translocations put a partner gene next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) on chromosome 14 and its strong promoter.

TranslocationGeneEffectLymphoma
t(8;14)MYCOncogene → rapid growthBurkitt
t(14;18)BCL2Blocks apoptosisFollicular
t(11;14)Cyclin D1Loss of cell-cycle controlMantle cell
t(11;18)API2-MALT1NF-κB activationMALT
t(2;5)NPM-ALKTyrosine kinaseAnaplastic large cell
Point mutationBRAF V600EKinase onHairy cell
AmplificationPD-L1/PD-L2Immune evasionHodgkin
In-house exam

The chromosome involved in most lymphoma translocations = 14 (IGH).

Memory tool

In order: 8;14 Burkitt → 11;14 Mantle → 11;18 MALT → 14;18 Follicular: "Burkitt Makes More Friends."

ApplyLO 2 application question

A1Flow cytometry shows CD19+, CD20+, CD5+, CD23− cells. What stain confirms the diagnosis?
Cyclin D1 (mantle cell, t(11;14)).

LO 3Low grade vs high grade

Q1. How do indolent and aggressive lymphomas differ?
Low grade / indolentHigh grade / aggressive
PatientOlder (>50)All ages incl. children; median 60
NodesMultiple, painlessSingle rapidly growing node or mass
SpreadMarrow + blood; extranodal rareExtranodal common (CNS, testis); blood rare
HistologyNon-destructive; small cells, clumped chromatinDiffuse, destructive; large cells, vesicular nuclei, nucleoli, many mitoses
OutcomeSlow, rarely curable; may transform → DLBCLFatal untreated, but chemo-sensitive, curable
Analogy — tortoise and hare

Chemo kills dividing cells. The hare (aggressive) divides constantly, so chemo catches it. The tortoise (indolent) barely divides and has already wandered everywhere, so it escapes.

Step 1 — transformation

Stable indolent disease, then a fast-growing node, B symptoms, ↑ LDH → transformation, usually to DLBCL: CLL (Richter, ~10%), follicular (30–50%, MYC), marginal zone, NLP Hodgkin.

Q2. What do the chronic leukemias look like under the microscope?

CLL

  • Small mature lymphocytes + smudge cells

CLL marrow

  • Nodular lymphoid aggregates

Hairy cell marrow

  • "Fried-egg" cells; dry tap

Mycosis fungoides

  • Pautrier microabscess in epidermis

ATLL

  • Clover-leaf (flower) cells
In-house exam
  • CLL: smudge cells and marrow nodules
  • Hairy cell: CD11c/25/103, BRAF
  • Mycosis fungoides: cerebriform nuclei, Pautrier abscess
Step 1

Hairy cell: TRAP+, dry tap (marrow fibrosis), treat with cladribine (purine analog).

Q3. What do the indolent B-cell lymphomas look like?

Follicular

  • Back-to-back follicles, thin mantles

BCL2 stain

  • Reactive follicle − (left) · follicular lymphoma + (right)

MALT

  • Lymphoepithelial lesions (cells invading glands)

Mantle cell

  • Monotonous small cells, vague nodules
In-house exam

Paratrabecular lymphoid aggregates in marrow → follicular. Reactive follicles are BCL2−; neoplastic follicles are BCL2+.

Q4. What do the aggressive lymphomas look like?

DLBCL

  • Sheets of large cells, prominent nucleoli

Burkitt

  • Starry sky: macrophages eating apoptotic debris

Bulky node

  • Rapidly growing mass (DLBCL)
In-house exam

Burkitt: starry sky, CD10/CD19/CD20/IgM, t(8;14), endemic = EBV + jaw.

LO 5Presentation, course and complications

Q1. How do the chronic B- and T-cell leukemias present?
DiseasePresentationCourse / complications
CLL / SLL>60; often incidental lymphocytosis; nodes, hepatosplenomegaly4–10 y by stage; hypogammaglobulinemia → infections; AIHA/ITP (10–15%); Richter → DLBCL; worse with del 11q/17p (TP53)
Hairy cellOlder men; splenomegaly, pancytopenia, no nodes; infectionsIndolent; responds to cladribine
Mycosis fungoides / SézaryPruritic patch → plaque → tumor; Sézary: circulating cells + erythrodermaVariable; systemic disease = poor
ATLLHTLV-1 (Japan, Caribbean); skin lesions, nodes, HSM, hypercalcemiaAggressive; HTLV-1 also causes myelopathy

Mycosis fungoides

  • Plaques that won't heal → biopsy
Trap

Hypercalcemia + bone lesions isn't always myeloma: with skin lesions and CD4+ T cells, think ATLL (HTLV-1). A small M-spike can occur in CLL.

Q2. How do the indolent B-cell lymphomas present?
DiseasePresentationCourse
FollicularOlder adults; painless bilateral cervical + axillary nodes, waxing-waning; fatigueIncurable, ~7–10 y; low-dose chemo; → DLBCL 30–50%
Marginal zone / MALTSites of chronic stimulation: stomach (H. pylori), salivary (Sjögren), thyroid (Hashimoto), small bowel (RLQ pain, wall thickening)Usually localized; gastric MALT regresses with H. pylori eradication (t(11;18) resists)
Mantle cellOlder men; diffuse nodes, HSM, GI polyposisIncurable, 3–5 y
LymphoplasmacyticIgM spike → hyperviscosity (vision, headache, neuropathy) = WaldenströmIndolent; plasmapheresis; no lytic lesions

Intestinal lymphoma

  • Bowel wall thickening, RLQ pain
In-house exam

Small bowel distention + asymmetric wall thickening → MALT. Stomach = most common GI lymphoma site; H. pylori ulcer → atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, lymphoid hyperplasia, gastric lymphoma.

Trap — follicular vs mantle

Both: older patient, generalized nodes. CD10+, CD5−, t(14;18) = follicular; CD5+, cyclin D1, t(11;14) = mantle.

Q3. How do the aggressive lymphomas present?
DiseasePresentationCourse
DLBCLMedian 60; rapidly growing bulky node or extranodal mass (GI, testis, Waldeyer ring, CNS)Fatal untreated; CR 60–80%, ~50% cured; MYC/bulky = worse
BurkittChildren/young adults; jaw (endemic, EBV) or ileocecal mass (sporadic) → obstruction, intussusceptionVery fast (~40% in S phase) but chemo-sensitive; tumor lysis
Anaplastic large cellChildren/young adults; ulcerated skin lesions, nodes, high feverAggressive; ALK+ better
In-house exam
  • HIV + HHV-8 + pleural/ascitic lymphoma without a mass → primary effusion lymphoma
  • AIDS + brain mass of CD20+ B cells → also EBV+ (primary CNS lymphoma)
Step 1

Tumor lysis: ↑K⁺, ↑PO₄³⁻, ↑uric acid, ↓Ca²⁺ → AKI. Prevent with hydration + allopurinol/rasburicase.

ApplyLO 4–5 application questions

A1A 55-year-old man has abdominal fullness, a huge spleen, no lymphadenopathy, Hb 4, WBC 1.2k and platelets 28k. Marrow aspirate is a dry tap. Diagnosis and mutation?
Hairy cell leukemia; BRAF V600E.
A2A 69-year-old with CLL stable for 10 years develops rapid splenic growth, anemia and B symptoms. What happened?
Richter transformation to DLBCL.
A3A 54-year-old woman with early satiety has small CD20+ cells infiltrating gastric glands; she improves after H. pylori therapy. Diagnosis?
Gastric MALT lymphoma.

LO 6–7Hodgkin classification and the Reed-Sternberg cell

Q1. What is Hodgkin lymphoma, and how is it classified?
  • Clonal B-cell lymphoma: few malignant cells (RS cells or variants) in a large background of lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells
  • Bimodal age: 15–40 and >50
  • Two families:
    • Classic (CD15+, CD30+): nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte rich, lymphocyte depleted
    • Nodular lymphocyte predominant (CD20+; CD15−, CD30−)
Q2. What does the Reed-Sternberg cell look like, and what are its variants?
  • Large, binucleate (or bilobed) with huge eosinophilic nucleoli: "owl's eyes"
  • From germinal center/post-GC B cells but lose B markers; CD15+, CD30+
  • Variants: lacunar (nodular sclerosis), pleomorphic (lymphocyte depleted), popcorn / L&H (NLP)

RS cell and variants

  • Binucleate "owl's eyes"

CD30

  • Membrane + Golgi dot

CD15

  • Positive in classic HL
In-house exam

RS cell = Hodgkin; markers CD15 and CD30. Guaranteed question.

Trap

RS-like cells occur in infectious mononucleosis and some NHLs: the right inflammatory background is required. CD30 alone also fits anaplastic large cell (T, ALK); classic HL adds CD15.

LO 8Pathogenesis and EBV

Q1. How do the RS cell and its background feed each other?
In-house exam

Transcription factor active in RS cells = NF-κB → uncontrolled cytokines.

Analogy — the owl in the crowd

A few owls (RS cells) shout for a crowd (cytokines); the crowd brings them food (growth factors). Most of the tumor is the crowd, not the owls.

Q2. What role does EBV play?
  • EBV is frequently found in RS cells, especially mixed cellularity and lymphocyte depleted; lymphocyte rich ~40%; nodular sclerosis uncommon; NLP negative
  • Prior infectious mononucleosis ↑ risk; workup includes testing for EBV
InfectionLymphoma
EBVEndemic Burkitt, Hodgkin (MC, LD), HIV/transplant DLBCL, primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS
HHV-8Primary effusion lymphoma (HIV)
HTLV-1ATLL
H. pyloriGastric MALT
HCVSplenic marginal zone, lymphoplasmacytic
In-house exam

HIV patient with EBV+ RS cells and few background lymphocytes → lymphocyte depleted.

LO 9The five Hodgkin subtypes

Q1. How do the subtypes compare?
SubtypePatientSites / stagePathologyEBVPrognosis
Nodular sclerosisMost common (65–70%); young adults, women ≈ menMediastinal, cervical, supraclavicular; earlyFibrous bands; lacunar cellsUncommonExcellent
Mixed cellularity2nd most common; older menAbdominal nodes, spleen; B symptoms; often advancedClassic RS in mixed lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cellsOften +Good
Lymphocyte richUncommon; olderEarlyClassic RS in a T-cell background~40%Very good
Lymphocyte depletedRarest; older, HIVAdvancedPleomorphic RS; few background cells+Worst
Nodular LP<5%; young–middle-aged menCervical/axillary; localizedPopcorn cells in B-cell nodules; CD20+, CD15/30−−Good (may → DLBCL)

Nodular sclerosis

  • Fibrous bands split the node

Mixed cellularity

  • RS cells in a mixed inflammatory background

Lymphocyte rich

  • Classic RS cells, T-cell background

Lymphocyte depleted

  • Pleomorphic RS, few lymphocytes

Nodular LP

  • Popcorn (L&H) cell
Memory tool

Nodular Sclerosis = Sisters, Sternum (mediastinum), Scars (bands). Mixed cellularity = Men with Many symptoms and Mono (EBV). Lymphocyte Depleted = lost Defense (HIV) → worst. Prognosis tracks lymphocytes: more = better.

Step 1

Young woman + anterior mediastinal mass + fibrous bands + lacunar cells → nodular sclerosis.

Trap — lymphocyte rich vs NLP

Both are full of lymphocytes. Lymphocyte rich has classic CD15/30 RS cells in a T-cell background; NLP has CD20+ popcorn cells in a B-cell background.

ApplyLO 9 application question

A1A 74-year-old man has fevers, weight loss, splenomegaly and mesenteric nodes. Biopsy shows lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils and binucleate CD15+/CD30+ cells. Subtype?
Mixed cellularity classic Hodgkin.

LO 10Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin

Q1. How do HL and NHL differ?
HodgkinNon-Hodgkin
Tumor cellFew RS cells among reactive cellsTumor cells make up the mass
AgeBimodal: young adults + >50Older (Burkitt in children)
NodesSingle group (cervical, mediastinal)Multiple peripheral
SpreadContiguous, orderlyNon-contiguous
Mesenteric / WaldeyerRareCommon
ExtranodalRareCommon
B symptomsCommon (+ pruritus)Less common
StagingCritical for prognosis and therapyHistologic type matters more
Memory tool

Hodgkin hops to the neighbor node; NHL parachutes anywhere.

Q2. How is lymphoma staged?
Ann Arbor stageExtent
IOne node region
II≥2 regions, same side of the diaphragm
IIIBoth sides of the diaphragm (± spleen)
IVDisseminated extranodal (liver, marrow, lung)
A / BB = fever, night sweats, >10% weight loss
  • Imaging stages the disease; most HL is caught early
  • HL outcome: radiation + chemo; early stage 75–90% curable
  • Adverse factors: stage IV, older age, B symptoms, bulky mediastinum, extensive spleen, multiple extranodal sites
Step 1 — late effects of HL therapy
  • Second cancers: AML/MDS (alkylators), NHL, breast cancer after mediastinal radiation, lung, thyroid, sarcoma
  • Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis; doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy
  • Accelerated atherosclerosis, hypothyroidism, infertility

ApplyLO 10 application question

A1A patient has involved cervical and mediastinal nodes plus night sweats; nothing below the diaphragm. Stage?
Stage IIB.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 70-year-old man has painless generalized lymphadenopathy and a WBC of 62,000/µL. The smear shows small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells. Flow cytometry will most likely show:

CLL/SLL: CD19/20 with CD5 and CD23.

2Most non-random translocations in B-cell lymphomas involve a gene on which chromosome?

IGH on chromosome 14 pairs with MYC, BCL2 or cyclin D1.

3A 61-year-old man has fatigue and painless bilateral cervical and axillary nodes. Biopsy shows crowded back-to-back follicles that stain BCL2+; marrow shows paratrabecular aggregates. The translocation is:

Follicular lymphoma: BCL2 next to IGH blocks apoptosis.

4A 55-year-old man has massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia and no lymphadenopathy. Marrow aspiration yields a dry tap. Which finding is expected?

Hairy cell leukemia. Teardrop cells and JAK2 would point to myelofibrosis instead.

5A 52-year-old man has a 6-month pruritic, scaly rash on his back that won't heal. Biopsy shows atypical CD4+ T cells with cerebriform nuclei clustered in the epidermis. Diagnosis?

Pautrier microabscesses; Sézary syndrome if cells circulate.

6A 4-year-old boy from equatorial Africa has a rapidly enlarging jaw mass. Biopsy shows sheets of intermediate cells with many mitoses and scattered macrophages containing debris. Which virus is associated?

Endemic Burkitt: starry sky, t(8;14), EBV.

7A 48-year-old man has right lower quadrant pain. CT shows focal small-bowel distention with asymmetric wall thickening. Biopsy shows small B cells invading glands. Most likely diagnosis?

Lymphoepithelial lesions → MALT.

8A 62-year-old man has an 11-cm ileal mass made of sheets of large CD19+/CD20+ cells with BCL6 rearrangement. Which statement about prognosis is correct?

DLBCL: fatal untreated, ~50% cured.

9A man with AIDS develops a pleural effusion containing large malignant lymphoid cells without a solid mass. Which virus is in the tumor cells?

Primary effusion lymphoma.

10A 24-year-old woman has a cough and an anterior mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows broad collagen bands and cells sitting in clear spaces. Diagnosis?

Fibrous bands + lacunar cells.

11Which transcription factor is constitutively active in Reed-Sternberg cells and drives cytokine release?

NF-κB → cytokines → inflammatory background.

12A 35-year-old man has a localized cervical node. Biopsy shows nodules of small B cells with scattered large cells with folded "popcorn" nuclei. Expected phenotype of the large cells?

Nodular lymphocyte predominant HL keeps B markers.

13Which feature favors Hodgkin over non-Hodgkin lymphoma?

HL spreads contiguously; staging guides therapy.

14A 40-year-old woman treated with chest radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 17 now has a breast mass. Most likely explanation?

Mediastinal radiation → breast cancer years later.
